# Book I, Proposition 14

*When two angles make a straight line*

> If with any straight line, and at a point on it, two straight lines not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles, the two straight lines will be in a straight line with one another.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/14-idea.svg" alt="If two angles side by side (red and yellow) together make two right angles, their outer arms (blue) join up into one straight line, never a bent one (dashed)." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>If two angles side by side (red and yellow) together make two right angles, their outer arms (blue) join up into one straight line, never a bent one (dashed).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/14.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.14, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For with any straight line AB, and at the point B on it, let the two straight lines BC, BD not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles ABC, ABD equal to two right angles;

I say that BD is in a straight line with CB.

For, if BD is not in a straight line with BC, let BE be in a straight line with CB.

Then, since the straight line AB stands on the straight line CBE,

the angles ABC, ABE are equal to two right angles. [I. 13]

But the angles ABC, ABD are also equal to two right angles;

therefore the angles CBA, ABE are equal to the angles CBA, ABD. [Post. 4 and C.N. 1]

Let the angle CBA be subtracted from each;

therefore the remaining angle ABE is equal to the remaining angle ABD, [C.N. 3]

the less to the greater: which is impossible.

Therefore BE is not in a straight line with CB.

Similarly we can prove that neither is any other straight line except BD.

Therefore CB is in a straight line with BD.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop14.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop14.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-! ## What Euclid reads off the figure -/

/-- A straight line through a point of `AB`, from a point `C` off it, crosses to
the other side: if `B` lies between `C` and `E`, then `E` is on the other side
of the straight line `AB` from `C`. (System E, Pasch 3) -/
theorem Prop14.opposite {A B C E : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (hCBE : Between C B E) :
    OppositeSidesOf C E A B := by
  obtain ⟨L, hA, hB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hABC.ne₁₂
  have hC : ¬ OnLine C L := hABC.off_line hA hB
  /- E is off AB too: a straight line through E and B goes on through C. -/
  have hE : ¬ OnLine E L := fun hE => hC (on_line_of_between (between_symm hCBE) hE hB)
  exact OppositeSidesOf.of_line hABC.ne₁₂ hA hB ⟨hC, hE, pasch3 hCBE hB⟩

/-- A straight line has only two sides: two points, each on the other side of
`AB` from `C`, are on the same side of `AB` as each other. (System E, Same
side 5) -/
theorem Prop14.sameSide {A B C D E : Point} (hD : OppositeSidesOf C D A B)
    (hE : OppositeSidesOf C E A B) : SameSideOf D E A B := by
  obtain ⟨L, hA, hB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hD.1
  obtain ⟨hC_L, hD_L, hCD⟩ := hD.oppositeSides hA hB
  obtain ⟨-, hE_L, hCE⟩ := hE.oppositeSides hA hB
  refine SameSideOf.of_line hD.1 hA hB ?_
  rcases same_side_or hC_L hD_L hE_L hCD with h | h
  · exact absurd h hCE
  · exact h

/-- "In a straight line with CB": if `CB` is produced beyond `B` to `E`, then any
point `D` on the ray from `B` through `E` lies in a straight line with `CB`, on
the far side of `B` from `C`. (System E's rules for "between") -/
theorem Prop14.straight {B C D E : Point} (hCBE : Between C B E) (hD : OnRay D B E) :
    Between C B D := by
  obtain ⟨-, hDB, ⟨L, hB, hE, hD_L⟩, hDBE⟩ := hD
  have hC : OnLine C L := on_line_of_between (between_symm hCBE) hE hB
  have hCD : C ≠ D := by
    rintro rfl
    exact hDBE hCBE
  /- Of the three points C, B, D on one straight line, one lies between the
     other two. If C did, or D, then B would lie between D and E, and D would
     be off the ray. -/
  rcases between_cases (ne_of_between hCBE) hDB.symm hCD hC hB hD_L with h | h | h
  · exact h
  · exact absurd (between_symm (between_of_between_right (between_symm hCBE) h)) hDBE
  · exact absurd (between_inner h hCBE) hDBE

/-- If with any straight line, and at a point on it, two straight lines not lying on the same side
make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles, the two straight lines will be in a straight
line with one another. -/
theorem Prop14 {A B C D : Point} (hCD : OppositeSidesOf C D A B) (h : ∠ A B C + ∠ A B D = ∟ + ∟) :
    Between C B D := by
  -- For with any straight line AB, and at the point B on it, let the two straight lines BC, BD
  -- not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles ABC, ABD equal to two right angles;
  /- "Not lying on the same side": C and D are on opposite sides of AB. So C is
     off AB, and ABC is a triangle. -/
  have hABC : Triangle A B C := hCD.triangle
  have hA_B : A ≠ B := hABC.ne₁₂
  have hC_B : C ≠ B := hABC.ne₂₃.symm
  -- I say that BD is in a straight line with CB.
  /- In Lean: B lies between C and D. -/
  -- For, if BD is not in a straight line with BC, let BE be in a straight line with CB.
  /- CB is produced beyond B to E [Post. 1, Post. 2], which is `produce` in Book
     Zero. Euclid's supposition then says that BE is another straight line than
     BD: that D is not on the ray from B through E. We follow his argument
     under that supposition, as far as the impossible. -/
  obtain ⟨E, hCBE⟩ := produce hC_B
  have other : ¬ OnRay D B E → False := by
    intro hD_BE
    -- Then, since the straight line AB stands on the straight line CBE,
    /- Stands on it, and is not part of it: A is off the straight line CE, for
       that line passes through B, and A, B, C are not on one straight line. -/
    have hA_CE : ¬ Collinear C E A := by
      rintro ⟨L, hC, hE, hA⟩
      exact hABC ⟨L, hA, on_line_of_between_ends hCBE hC hE, hC⟩
    -- the angles ABC, ABE are equal to two right angles. [I. 13]
    have hCBA_ABE : ∠ C B A + ∠ A B E = ∟ + ∟ := Prop13 hCBE hA_CE
    -- But the angles ABC, ABD are also equal to two right angles;
    have hCBA_ABD : ∠ C B A + ∠ A B D = ∟ + ∟ := by
      rw [← angle_symm hA_B hC_B]
      exact h
    -- therefore the angles CBA, ABE are equal to the angles CBA, ABD. [Post. 4 and C.N. 1]
    /- Todhunter's point, which Heath reports: C.N. 1 is not enough by itself,
       for the two right angles of I.13 need not be the two of our hypothesis,
       and it is Postulate 4 that makes all right angles equal. In Lean,
       Postulate 4 has done its work before we get here: every right angle is
       written with the one name `∟`, and I.13 hands its two back as `∟ + ∟`.
       So the step itself is C.N. 1 alone. -/
    have hsum : ∠ C B A + ∠ A B E = ∠ C B A + ∠ A B D := CommonNotion1 hCBA_ABE hCBA_ABD
    -- Let the angle CBA be subtracted from each;
    -- therefore the remaining angle ABE is equal to the remaining angle ABD, [C.N. 3]
    have hABE_ABD : ∠ A B E = ∠ A B D :=
      CommonNotion3 (c := ∠ C B A) (d := ∠ C B A) (by rw [add_comm, hsum, add_comm]) rfl
    -- the less to the greater: which is impossible.
    /- In Euclid's figure BE falls within the angle ABD, so that ABE is a part
       of ABD; Lean must allow too for BD falling within ABE. Both figures are
       settled by `onRay_of_angle_eq` in Book Zero: on one side of a straight
       line, only one ray from a point of it makes a given angle with it, for
       otherwise one of two equal angles would be a part of the other, the less
       equal to the greater. E and D are on the same side of AB, both being on
       the other side from C (`Prop14.opposite`, `Prop14.sameSide`); so D would
       lie on the ray from B through E, against the supposition. -/
    have hDE : SameSideOf D E A B := Prop14.sameSide hCD (Prop14.opposite hABC hCBE)
    exact hD_BE (onRay_of_angle_eq hDE.swap hABE_ABD.symm)
  -- Therefore BE is not in a straight line with CB.
  /- That is, BE is not another straight line than BD: the supposition has
     failed, so D lies on the ray from B through E. -/
  have hD_BE : OnRay D B E := Classical.byContradiction other
  -- Similarly we can prove that neither is any other straight line except BD.
  /- Lean needs no "similarly": E was any point on CB produced, and the
     argument never asked which. -/
  -- Therefore CB is in a straight line with BD.
  exact Prop14.straight hCBE hD_BE
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

**I.13 turned round.** I.13 says that a straight line standing on a straight line makes angles equal to two right angles; I.14 says that two angles equal to two right angles, side by side, put their outer arms in one straight line. Euclid proves it by *reductio ad absurdum*, as in I.6. He supposes that BD is not in a straight line with CB, produces CB to E, and finds the angle ABE equal to the angle ABD, "the less to the greater: which is impossible." In Lean the supposition becomes "D is not on the ray from B through E", the argument runs as a sub-proof under it, and `Classical.byContradiction` turns its failure into "D does lie on that ray", from which `Prop14.straight` gives the conclusion. Producing CB is `produce` in Book Zero, so Postulates 1 and 2 are on the certificate, though Euclid gives no bracket there. Later, I.45 and I.47 will lean on I.14 to show that two straight lines they have built are one.

**"Not lying on the same side."** The condition matters, and Heath, following Proclus, says why: "two straight lines on the *same* side of another straight line and meeting it in one and the same point may make with one and the same portion of the straight line terminated at the point two angles which are together equal to two right angles, in which case however the two straight lines would not be in a straight line with one another." Proclus quotes a construction from Porphyry, with angles of half a right angle and one and a half right angles, though Heath adds that "there is no particular value in the construction" (vol. 1, p. 277). In Lean the condition is the hypothesis `OppositeSidesOf C D A B`, and it is used exactly once: to put D on the same side of AB as E, where the last step needs it.

**Post. 4 and C.N. 1.** Heath: "Todhunter points out that for the inference in this line Post. 4, that all right angles are equal, is necessary as well as the Common Notion that things which are equal to the same thing (or rather, here, to *equal things*) are equal. A similar remark applies to steps in the proofs of I. 15 and I. 28" (vol. 1, p. 277). In Lean, Postulate 4 has done its work before I.14 begins: every right angle is written with the one name `∟`, the size Postulate 4 says they all share, and I.13 hands its two right angles back as `∟ + ∟`. So the step itself is `CommonNotion1`, and the subtraction that follows is `CommonNotion3`.

**The less to the greater.** In Euclid's figure BE falls within the angle ABD, so the angle ABE is a part of the angle ABD and cannot be equal to it. Lean has to allow for the other figure too, in which BD falls within ABE. Both are settled by `onRay_of_angle_eq` in Book Zero, the fact that I.4 already used to lay AC along DF: on one side of a straight line, only one ray from a point of it makes a given angle with it. Its proof is Euclid's argument here in general form. System E's Triple incidence 2 says which ray lies within the other's angle, Diagram-angle 2 makes that angle a whole of two parts, and Common Notion 5 makes the whole greater than the part. Heath's figure, as a figure for a *reductio* often must, does not show what is supposed. It draws CBD straight, as it really is, and BE bent away from it. The Lean argues from the figure as supposed: E on CB produced, and D off the ray BE.

**What Lean made us say.** Three facts Euclid reads off his figure are helper theorems in the file. `Prop14.opposite`: since B lies between C and E, the straight line AB separates them, so E is on the other side of AB from C (System E, Pasch 3). `Prop14.sameSide`: a straight line has only two sides, so E and D, each on the other side from C, are on the same side as each other (Same side 5). And `Prop14.straight`: a point on the ray from B through E is in a straight line with CB, which is the last step from "D lies along BE" to "B lies between C and D". One more small fact sits inside the proof, the word "stands": I.13 needs A off the straight line CBE, which holds because A, B, C are not on one straight line. Every rule cited is one of Jeremy Avigad, Edward Dean and John Mumma's in System E, read, as always, with LeanEuclid's careful Lean version open alongside.

**"Similarly we can prove."** Euclid refutes one rival straight line BE and then says the same goes for "any other straight line except BD". Heath notes that "the Greek expresses this by the future of the verb, δείξομεν, 'we shall prove,' which however would perhaps be misleading in English" (vol. 1, p. 277). Lean needs no "similarly": E was any point at all on CB produced, and the argument never asked which. Heath's notes on I.14 open with a translator's confession, too: "There is no greater difficulty in translating the works of the Greek geometers than that of accurately giving the force of prepositions." The one word πρός, in this one enunciation, has to be rendered "with", "at" and "on" (vol. 1, p. 277).

**The modern way.** Put B at 0 and A at 1 in the complex plane, and C = r e^{iθ} above the real axis. Then D, below it and making the angle π − θ with BA, is s e^{−i(π − θ)} = −s e^{iθ}, a negative real multiple of C, so B lies between C and D. Had D been above the axis, it would be s e^{i(π − θ)} = −s e^{−iθ}, the mirror image of that point, and in general not in line with C at all: that is Proclus' warning.
